Simple Present, Present Continuous, Be Going to in Affirmative

You use the simple present tense to talk about routines or facts. You use the present continuous tense to describe actions that are developing at a particular period of time. Finally, you use be going to to express actions in a near future.
A tree list consists in carrying out the data organization in a hierarchical order through a root node and sub nodes.

Simple present tense

You use this tense to talk about things that you generally do, like your daily routines. You also use this tense to talk about general truths or facts.

 

Structure:

Subject + verb* + complement

 

*Remember that for the third person of the singular (he, she, and it), you need to add an “s” “es” or “ies” to the verb.

 

Examples:

A stack list works according to the order of access, or the LIFO order.

On the contrary, queue lists execute the order FIFO.

 

Present continuous tense

You use this tense to talk about things that are happening at the moment we are speaking.

 

Structure:

Subject + to be verb + main verb+ ing + complement

 

Example:

My computer system is organizing data in a stack list.

 

Be going to

You use this tense to express future plans and intentions.

 

Structure:

Subject + to be verb + going to + main verb in base verb + complement

 

Example:

A queue list is going to work through a FIFO order.
In other words, the computer program is storing and retrieving data items constantly.

images.text: Professor Moore: Good evening, everyone! Thanks for coming to this lecture about data structures. In this opportunity, we are discussing different types of data structures. You're going to learn valuable information, so I suggest taking notes about it. Let's start. As you know, a data structure is the particular organization of data in a computer program. Depending on the type of information your computer needs to categorize, you are going to use a different type of data structure. The two common types computer science is using nowadays are arrays and types of lists.

Concerning the arrays, they are basic data types that haven't any internal links between their elements, so it's necessary that all data belongs to the same type. It stores data in addressable locations sequentially. In other words, the computer program is storing and retrieving data items constantly. On the other hand, regarding the types of lists, unlike the arrays, they have one or more pointers to link their elements. As their name suggests, there is a strong tendency to work with specialized lists in this type of data structures. Among the types of specialized lists, we have trees, stacks, and queues.

A tree list consists in carrying out the data organization in a hierarchical order through a root node and sub nodes. When your computer is executing this type of list, it speeds important functions like “inserting” or “deleting”. With regard to stacks, they work according to the order of access, or the LIFO order (last in, first out). It means the last item the program inserts is going to be at the top, removing the previous item. On the contrary, queues execute the order FIFO (first in, first out); that's to say, the last item the program inserts is going to be at the end, and the one to solve is going to be the first in the queue. This type of list plays a part when there are specific tasks that need special attention.

To conclude, I invite you to summarize the most important aspects of this lecture in some meaningful phrases. I really enjoyed giving this lecture tonight. Keep reading about arrays and lists. You can also practice surfing the web to get more examples and information.
